question: Why do medications absorb so slowly when given as an intradermal injection?

options.A: The body attacks the drug before it can dissolve
options.B: The dermal layer has a very limited blood supply
options.C: The needle gauge is too small to release much fluid
options.D: The outer layer of skin blocks fluid movement

explanation: You've got this! The dermis doesn't have as many blood vessels as other layers, which is actually a good thing—it keeps the medication right where we put it for tests like Mantoux. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why do we choose the intradermal route instead of subcutaneous for allergy skin tests?

options.A: It allows safe observation of a localized skin response
options.B: It triggers a rapid whole-body immune reaction
options.C: It is completely painless for the patient
options.D: It delivers a larger volume of testing solution

explanation: Great job! Intradermal injections let us easily watch how the skin reacts locally to allergens or TB tests without spreading the solution all over the body. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h1)

question: What is the most common and preferred site for giving an intradermal injection?

options.A: Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
options.C: Deltoid muscle of the upper arm

explanation: Spot on! The inner forearm is easy to reach, has very little hair, and lets you clearly see any skin reactions. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h2)

question: Why must you let the alcohol skin cleanser dry completely before giving an intradermal injection?

options.A: To stop stinging pain caused by wet alcohol entering the puncture
options.B: To prevent the antiseptic from neutralizing the medication
options.C: To make the outer skin layer tough enough for the needle
options.D: To ensure the skin surface remains completely sterile

explanation: Thinking like a caring nurse! Letting the alcohol dry saves your patient from a sharp, unnecessary burning pain when the needle goes in. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the best needle size for an intradermal injection?
explanation: You're getting the hang of this! A fine, short needle ensures the medicine stays shallow in the dermis rather than slipping into the fat below. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h3)

question: What is the maximum amount of medication you should give in a single intradermal injection site?
explanation: Correct! The dermis is a tight little space. If you push more than 0.5 mL in there, it will either damage the tissue or leak right out. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h3)

question: At what angle should you insert the needle for an intradermal injection?
explanation: Awesome! A shallow 10 to 15-degree angle is the secret to keeping that needle tip resting nicely right inside the thin dermal layer. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why do you pull the skin taut instead of pinching it before an intradermal injection?

options.A: Taut skin makes the needle sharper as it enters
options.B: Pinching causes severe bruising around the injection site
options.C: Pinching the skin lifts it and accidentally creates a subcutaneous pocket
options.D: Pulling the skin taut numbs the nerve endings temporarily

explanation: Well done! Pinching bunches up the fatty layer underneath, making it way too easy to accidentally slide past the dermis. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h4)

question: When must a patient come back to have a Mantoux tuberculin skin test read?
explanation: Spot on! This 48 to 72-hour window gives the body enough time to build a visible immune reaction for us to measure accurately. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h5)

question: When reading a skin test, which specific physical change should you measure?
explanation: You nailed it! We measure induration (the hard, raised bump) because that shows a true immune response, whereas simple surface redness doesn't mean a positive result. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h5)
